title: AI godfather Yann LeCun torches Anthropic CEO over AI gatekeeping
summary: ‘It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma,’ he says
content: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is taking heat from AI luminary Yann LeCun, one of the founding fathers of modern machine learning, because of the Claudefather's fear-mongering around open-weights models, which also happen to compete with his products. In an X post this week, LeCun likened the Amodei's advocacy to a “new form of medieval obscurantism.” “Dario’s spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal, and he would stay in control,” LeCun wrote in response to a now three-year-old video posted to the platform in which Amodei warned US Congress members about the dangers of open-weights models, the use of which could not be monitored or policed. “He left OpenAI because he wasn’t going to have control. It’s like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.” LeCun is one of the most influential names in AI and ML. His team is credited with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in the late ’80s during his time at Bell Labs. He later oversaw the development of Meta’s Llama herd of models as chief AI scientist before shifting gears away from LLMs to world model architectures like JEPA. He has also been a strong proponent of open source AI development and open models. Of the major model houses, Anthropic has taken the most hostile position against the adoption of open-weights models. Despite advocating against the unregulated diffusion of open models for years, Anthropic’s fearmonger-in-chief has maintained that the company isn’t opposed to them. “Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post earlier this year. The executive has instead fomented fears over their potential misuse. “Open-weights models — it does not matter whether they come from China or anywhere else — do potentially present a higher risk than closed models, because it is very difficult to apply guardrails to them or monitor their usage, and, once weights are released, they cannot be withdrawn,” the blog post read. Amodei has repeatedly hammered these talking points over the past several years, including in the Senate hearing that solicited LeCun’s post. Amodei has also called for measures, such as stricter export controls on the export of high-end accelerators to China; a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation operations, for which his company has previously accused Alibaba and other Chinese model devs; and mandating safety testing for sufficiently advanced open-weights models. In other words, Anthropic doesn’t want all freely downloadable models banned, just the ones that Amodei thinks aren’t playing fair or are powerful enough to compete with its own. LeCun isn’t the only one who has pushed back against anti-open-weights rhetoric in recent memory. Earlier this summer, a cadre of tech titans, including Meta, Microsoft, IBM, Dell, and Nvidia, wrote an open letter [ PDF ] in support of open-weights models. Open models “strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the time. “The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.” As we previously reported , Nvidia’s future depends on its ability to sell to a diverse set of customers ranging from the big model houses like Anthropic and OpenAI to public clouds, neoclouds, and enterprises. And while many of these companies are perfectly happy to get their AI through Claude or ChatGPT, others, whether it be for regulatory or cost reasons, are not. Earlier this month, we reported how British neobank Revolut cut their vibe coding tab by 10x by moving its roughly 2,000 employees from Claude to Z.AI’s GLM 5.1 running on a cluster of 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. The problem for Anthropic, and OpenAI for that matter, is the more enterprises that embrace open-weights models, the less likely they are to spring for Claude or ChatGPT. The Register reached out to Anthropic for comment, but had not heard back at the time of publication. ®

title: Anthropic says Claude solved an age-old math problem, but the written proof is 250,000 pages of slop
summary: If the AI can't explain what it's proven, are we actually any closer to understanding?
content: The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe. But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box? That question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure. In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so important that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them. The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2. Confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here . What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution. Researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros . There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that. Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate. The four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs. The Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. For Clay to consider the problem solved and award the prize, the proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, remain available for scrutiny for at least two years, and receive broad acceptance from the mathematics community. As it stands, Alpöge describes the 250,000 pages of text generated by the model for its written proof as a “massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop.’” Not long after Alpöge's remarks and Lean code were published, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil released a nearly 1,000-page draft proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, who earned his PhD at Stanford in 2020. Masullo has reportedly spent more than a decade pursuing the problem. Frameworks like Lean make mathematics a prime candidate for AI-assisted discovery for many of the same reasons that the technology has proven so successful in software development: code either compiles and runs or it doesn’t. Code can also be audited and could, with great effort, be deciphered. But a proof written in Lean isn't a mathematical proof in the traditional, human-readable sense. Although its logical validity can be checked by a computer, understanding the reasoning behind it can be another matter. Traditional proofs ideally explain their arguments in a way that other mathematicians can follow. Cantor's Diagonal Argument offers a comparatively accessible example. While the clock hasn’t even started for the Clay Math Institute, the Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative have already declared the Riemann Hypothesis solved. “We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the orgs wrote in a joint statement. “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.” Even if the code ends up being right, if we still don’t know why it’s true, have we really learned anything meaningful? "At the minute, we don't even know why the theorem is true," Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said in a recent Al Jazeera interview. Alpöge’s proof may simply be the product of a black box. To quote the late Arthur C Clarke, “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.” The implications of such a technology aren’t lost on researchers. Months ago, several prominent researchers called for greater scrutiny and oversight regarding the application of AI in mathematics. “Mathematics produces not only a body of results, but also understanding, clarity, and judgment among the communities of mathematicians who have shaped them, often in the context of their own autonomously guided research,” the Leiden Declaration reads. “This expert knowledge is essential, both to effectively use mathematics, and to continue to articulate new and significant research questions.” ®

title: Claude Ship puts AI at the helm of pull request approvals
summary: Tired of waiting for a meatbag to approve a change? Anthropic has an agent for that
content: Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship to review, fix, and approve pull requests (PRs), offering more AI automation to help teams handle the output of AI coding tools. Claude Ship combines the generally available Code Review service with two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. It is available to Claude Team and Enterprise customers using GitHub repositories. Anthropic said : "On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too." Its stated goal is to "ship code as fast as teams write it." One consequence of the AI coding revolution is the sheer amount of agent output, which requires review and approval before going live. Claude Ship is one way to address that by automating more of the workflow. PR Steward works through failing continuous integration (CI) checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback. Claude Approvals can actually approve a PR, something that might rattle the nerves of some engineers. Claude Approvals applies an approval policy, written by the team as a file in the repository. "Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios," Anthropic said. The company advised caution: "For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light." While developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests (depending on their permissions and the repository's branch rules) with a /ship command in Claude Code, administrators can set up the rules on a repository-by-repository basis. "Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off," Anthropic said. "Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it." The extra automation also brings extra charges. Usage is token-based, and even observe-only approval policies can incur costs if they invoke classifiers or Code Review. Anthropic also includes the familiar disclaimer: "Claude Ship uses AI and may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues." The Register spoke to an engineer who works for a company that uses Claude. They were a little cynical about the whole thing, saying: "It just seems like a glorification of what I already use Claude on – git merge or git rebase. "Our golden rule so far with Git is to limit Claude to read operations there; this layer of separation still lets devs stay in control and allows them a judgment of the AI changes – what to keep, tweak, or commit. "If that's offloaded to Claude and it has Git history-rewrite access, the devs will lose that overview and judgment opportunity." How much authority Claude receives depends on the organization's configuration. Approval is not the same as merging, and existing branch protections and required checks still apply. Anthropic's answer to a growing queue of AI-generated changes is more AI. Teams still have to decide which decisions they're prepared to delegate. ®

title: UK gov invests in defense startup making virtual training ground for AI
summary: Britain wants sovereign capability to test whether military AI will work before it gets deployed for real
content: The British government is investing in a UK-based AI defense startup that aims to train autonomous military systems in virtual environments, in a bid to reduce the country's reliance on overseas technology. Both the Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) have contributed to a Series A funding round for Agon Dynamics, said to value the biz at $450 million. This $70 million round takes the total capital raised by the firm to $100 million, following its initial $30 million seed round earlier this year. The government claims this move will help strengthen the UK’s sovereign capabilities when it comes to the use of AI for defense, plus the hope that nurturing native technical know-how converts into industrial strength and greater resilience. But it is not revealing how much cash it has stumped up, claiming such investments are commercially sensitive, although it did say that typical equity amounts obtained from the the Sovereign AI Fund tend to be worth around £1 million to £10 million ($1.3 million to $13 million). Agon is understood to be developing facilities to train and test AI systems needed for defense. This covers systems to help defend against drone attacks, or ensuring that AI tools still continue to work as intended if communications with the command center are disrupted. Training like this currently needs to be carried out in the real world, which is time-consuming and expensive, according to the government. For this reason, Agon is building a "virtual battlefield" environment where AI models can be tested against realistic simulations of the situations they might encounter. The company says its synthetic battle arena provides a safe, repeatable environment for developers and defense contractors to try out autonomous systems against thousands of demanding scenarios before deployment. Systems can face adaptive virtual adversaries informed by live conflict intelligence, helping them to respond to evolving tactics, threats and operating conditions. This may include simulations of mass drone attacks that would overwhelm conventional air defense systems, or testing how autonomous systems operate when navigation is degraded or adversary tactics change. "Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match," says co-founder and CEO Tristam Constant, a former British Army officer. "We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defense systems, in Europe, for Europe - to outperform adversary capabilities." For the government, AI Minister Kanishka Narayan claimed that Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure such technologies are reliable, trustworthy, and deployed responsibly. "AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era," he stated. ®

title: Education software supplier's legacy login system left 355,000 school email addresses exposed
summary: Have I Been Pwned puts a number on September's attack on Bromcom
content: More than 355,000 school staff and pupil email addresses ended up in the hands of hackers who broke into UK education software supplier Bromcom in September. The breach was added to Have I Been Pwned on Monday, revealing that 355,051 unique email addresses were caught up in the incident. The data also included single sign-on (SSO) registration reference numbers, although Bromcom insists that no passwords or authentication tokens were stolen. As The Register reported in Octobe r , the attackers got in through a legacy SSO registration component in Bromcom's Communications Server environment. The technology had already been superseded but was still running because an internal system continued to use it. Bromcom discovered something was amiss on September 6 after customers reported problems accessing its SSO service. At the time, the company was still working with external forensic specialists to establish exactly what the intruders had managed to get their hands on. Bromcom's FAQ says its investigation is complete and confirms that the intruders used a script to extract SSO registration information from the compromised server. The supplier insists its Management Information System (MIS), used by schools to keep track of everything from attendance to pupil records, was untouched. The compromised service also couldn't be used to get into Microsoft or Google accounts, which have their own login systems. Bromcom has since pulled the plug on the old component, tightened its authorization checks, and added more security logging. It says it hasn't found any evidence of accounts being hijacked as a result of the breach. Bromcom also confirmed it hadn't reported the breach to the UK's Information Commission's Office. Its reasoning is that it was the data processor, not the controller, so any decision to involve the regulator was for the affected schools and academy trusts to make. As for the risk to staff and pupils, Bromcom considers it to be low. No passwords or pupil records held in the MIS were taken, it says, although schools have been advised to watch for phishing messages and suspicious requests to reset passwords or approve sign-ins. The supplier's software is used by more than 5,000 schools and 390 multi-academy trusts across the UK, though it hasn't said how many were caught up in this particular mess. The Register has asked Bromcom how many schools and pupils were affected, and whether the figure published by Have I Been Pwned matches its own findings, but has yet to receive a response. Bromcom kept the superseded component running because an internal system still needed it. Unfortunately, the intruders found a use for it too. ®

title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
summary: EU Academy names and email addresses exposed, with users warned via website notice rather than contacted directly
content: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday , Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday , almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

title: Microsoft brings serverless PostgreSQL into Fabric to bridge transactions and analytics
summary: HorizonDB preview follows rivals' moves, with analysts warning tighter integration could make an eventual exit harder
content: Microsoft has brought its HorizonDB PostgreSQL service into public preview in Fabric, aiming to bring transactional and analytical workloads closer together. The corporation says applications can submit queries through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, with transactional and analytical work handled by the appropriate engines. Analysts said the move follows similar efforts by Databricks and Snowflake to combine operational databases with analytics. But tighter integration with Microsoft's stack could make applications harder to move elsewhere. Fabric HorizonDB joins SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft's Fabric database portfolio. "By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps," Microsoft said. Microsoft first unveiled Azure HorizonDB in preview in November 2025 and made it generally available last week. It competes with other cloud database services and distributed systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, both of which support PostgreSQL's wire protocol. At the time, it said HorizonDB would offer "massive read scale without the need to replicate the database between instances." Speaking to The Register last week, Shireesh Thota, veep of Azure databases and Fabric applications, said that bringing the system into Fabric – its platform for data lakes, data warehouses, and analytics launched in 2023 – would connect operational data in HorizonDB with analytical data in OneLake, Fabric's unified data lake. "Once the data hits the OneLake storage, you can have analytical engines that take advantage of it. In HorizonDB, the PostgreSQL query engine can talk to the distributed query engine that we use in our Fabric data warehouse. We're fusing these query engines, thereby enabling the developers to submit a query that has pieces of the query that can work on OLTP and pieces of the query that can work on OLAP," he said. "The application need not worry about two endpoints, or about consistency of data and all that complexity. They can just talk to HorizonDB as a Fabric endpoint, and they can submit all these queries. We are basically operationalizing in OneLake." Operational data remains in HorizonDB's database storage, while mirroring maintains an analytical copy in OneLake, introduced in 2023 , which replicates a snapshot of the external database to OneLake in Delta Parquet tables and keeps the replica synced in "near real time." Thota said the process would not affect the transactional system. "Our core goal is to never impact OLTP workload while we are doing this, and we succeed [by] reading off the log as an additional replica to do this mirroring," he said. But the overall plan of putting serverless PostgreSQL OLTP in an analytics platform, bringing it close to OLAP systems, is one some vendors are already executing to meet the demands of new AI agent-led workloads. Adam Ronthal, research veep in Gartner's Data and Analytics Group, said: "The addition of Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB follows the 2025 acquisitions of PostgreSQL vendors by Databricks – Neon – and Snowflake – Crunchy. It delivers a high-performance, serverless operational RDBMS that is tightly coupled with Microsoft's lakehouse offering and well-suited to the ephemeral demands of AI agents. "Competing directly with AWS Aurora and Google Cloud's AlloyDB, HorizonDB acts as a foundational serving layer for the next generation of AI- and analytics-infused applications. For organizations aligned with Azure and Fabric, it provides an industry-standard PostgreSQL foundation for AI development." Andrew Snodgrass, research vice president of analyst company Directions on Microsoft, said the announcement of HorizonDB in Fabric was a "surprise," although "a watered-down version" compared to the version of the serverless database that became generally available on Azure last week. "It joins (document database) CosmosDB in Fabric and SQL database (based on the SQL Server engine) in Fabric. It highlights that Microsoft is still focused on making Fabric the data hub of their universe." HorizonDB – both in Azure and Fabric – is a PostgreSQL service which Microsoft says has 100 percent compatibility with the open source system that has enjoyed a meteoric rise over the last decade. The support for PostgreSQL has led some to question the software giant's commitment to its own proprietary OLTP system, SQL Server. Thota pointed out that the SQL database , based on the SQL Server engine, is already available in Fabric. Microsoft is also evaluating similar integration for that service, although he gave no timetable. "We are just beginning this journey, and most of the innovation is neutral to PostgreSQL and SQL. Some of it would be particular to how the individual query engine fuses with the analytical query engine. PostgreSQL does it slightly differently than SQL, but the idea is that most of the work is neutral. We are evaluating that work as well. I don't have timelines for that, but it is certainly in our thinking," he said. Nonetheless, Holger Mueller, principal analyst at Constellation Research, said it was good to see Microsoft go all in on support of open source. "In general, it is an acknowledgement that they cannot win the battle for the SQL database with SQL Server – as it is as proprietary as the leader Oracle – and now they bank on the openness of PostgreSQL as another approach," he said. However, using HorizonDB integrated into the Fabric/Azure stack may create so many dependencies with Microsoft's technology that lock-in to the vendor will remain a risk. "The primary concerns of open source – scale and support – have been eliminated by Microsoft's commitment and by now track record... the challenges are the embeddings of HorizonDB into the bigger Microsoft stack – which will make portability hard again. But every vendor wants and provides stickiness – clothed in ease of use and lower TCO," Mueller said. ®

title: FCC proposes 'tit-for-tat' restrictions on foreign satellite operators
summary: December vote would launch rulemaking to mirror barriers facing US providers abroad, with EU spectrum plans in the crosshairs
content: The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote in December on proposals [PDF] that would restrict foreign satellite operators in the same way their home countries restrict US providers. The telecoms regulator says the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators. The main aim appears to be hitting back at European efforts to build up the region's own space communications industries. According to the FCC, the US has so far welcomed satellite systems licensed abroad on a level playing field, but that regulators elsewhere have begun holding US systems to different rules than they apply to their own domestic suppliers. "This has operated to the disadvantage of American satellite providers that are or may be burdened with regulatory and spectrum limitations that their competitors in foreign nations simply do not face," said FCC chairman Brendan Carr. The FCC has singled out the EU's Digital Networks Act , which proposes harmonized connectivity rules across the bloc. A separate proposal would overhaul authorization for mobile satellite services (MSS) in the 2 GHz band after existing rights expire in May 2027. Earlier this year, the FCC laid out some of its concerns, saying that EU-wide authorization of satellite spectrum would replace the national licensing by member states "with which US satellite operators have become accustomed," and could require wholesale relicensing of any US systems operating in Europe. "The FCC voting on foreign satellite companies is consistent with the Digital Networks Act, but is more of a response to the EU's decisions on how it plans to allocate the EU-wide 2 GHz spectrum," CCS Insight analyst Joe Gardiner told The Register . "The EU outlined in its proposal that, for two-thirds of the spectrum, only operators based in the EU with EU ownership and aligned with the EU's strategic goals will be considered for the spectrum. "This has locked out companies like SpaceX and Amazon Leo from attaining access to spectrum that is highly valuable for satellite direct-to-device services. The US government is looking to retaliate, to support the US constellations that would have attempted to win this EU-wide spectrum." Following an initial consultation in March, the FCC will vote in December on opening a rulemaking to reconsider how foreign-licensed satellite operators gain access to the US market. "It is time for this regulatory asymmetry to end," Carr said, adding that the FCC now proposes to mirror any regulations that foreign nations apply to American satellite providers. "If there are limits or restrictions on American providers operating abroad, then the notice proposes to apply those or similar regulatory restraints to satellite providers from those countries that are operating here." Britain is outside the EU, but does not escape the FCC's ire. The agency previously claimed the UK Space Agency allocates a significant portion of its budget, circa 75 percent in 2023/24, to European Space Agency (ESA) procurements, which US companies are not allowed to bid for as America is not a member of ESA. British satellite operators could therefore face restrictions on access to the US market if the FCC adopts reciprocal measures. The UK's space industry generated £18.6 billion in income in 2022/23, according to the UK Space Agency. ®

title: InferNode gives Bell Labs' Inferno OS a 64-bit second wind
summary: Plan 9's successor finds a new role containing AI agents, though its developer says those features are optional
content: InferNode brings a modernized, 64-bit edition of Inferno, the distributed operating system that followed Plan 9 from Bell Labs. For us, the strapline of the InferNode project distracts from the interesting part. It describes the project as a "Secure Runtime for AI Agents," but we think it's something far more interesting than another LLM tool. Fair warning: this vulture has no interest whatsoever in AI agents, and we are not even going to look at this planned use of InferNode. We're interested in the OS, and here, its GitHub repository spells out the part that caught our attention: "a 64-bit Inferno® OS." That grabbed us because Inferno is a very interesting OS, although it doesn't get much attention – for example, the official Inferno GitHub repository shows little activity in the last few years. Inferno is the successor to Plan 9, which we've written and talked about before , including recent releases of its community continuation, 9front . Plan 9 is what the team who invented Unix did next. Plan 9 is a very minimalist, natively clustered Unix: machines can freely mount one another's filesystems, display windows on one another, and start processes on one another. Plan 9 turns a network of machines running this Unix-like OS into a single machine. So, for instance, if you were working on a laptop with limited storage and compute power, you could compile a large complex project on a faster machine elsewhere on the network, using project files located on a third machine, while watching the process in your terminal on your screen, with no messing about with SSH sessions. Plan 9 and 9front programs are compiled into architecture-specific native binaries. Different processor families can still work together across the network, but the same executable won't run unchanged on both an x86-64 laptop and an Arm64 server. Inferno takes a different approach. It's contemporaneous with the far less ambitious Java. On Inferno, languages compile code for a VM called Dis, which is part of the kernel. This means that Inferno binaries execute directly on anything that the Inferno kernel runs on. The OS kernel is built to run bare-metal, or as a process on various other OSes, without needing a separate hardware virtual machine or hypervisor. A single binary can run on all supported CPU architectures. Inferno applications are normally written in the Limbo programming language , whose documentation was written by Unix co-creator Dennis Ritchie. Limbo is one of the languages that influenced Go, but Inferno lets compilers for other languages target Dis as well. The binaries run anywhere. Inferno on Arm, or x86, or RISC-V, or running in a Windows or Linux or macOS process, your program just runs. We've been trying to contact Vita Nuova , the company that maintains Inferno, for some years without success. Development appears to have slowed considerably. Moving the runtime to 64-bit also raises compatibility questions: some forks change Dis's word size and cannot run existing 32-bit bytecode unchanged. We're aware of several efforts to build 64-bit versions of Inferno. Caerwyn Jones's Inferno64 is one of the more visible, and the GitHub repository (and indeed his X account ) show considerable activity. However, Inferno64's Dis is not compatible with 32-bit Dis code. Another fork is Dinsmoor's Inferno64 , which also shows recent activity, albeit with the assistance of the Claude LLM. Others include the long-quiescent Purgatorio and 9ferno , both inactive for years, plus Scott Guyon's more active fork . Dropping the compatibility goal altogether, Node9 replaces Limbo with Lua and Dis with LuaJIT . There are more forks and variants than we've gone into here. Given that there have been quite a few efforts, and most haven't delivered final ready-to-use products yet, we were surprised when InferNode was suddenly announced on the Inferno-OS mailing list last week. Developer Peter Finn said: "An experimental runtime for containing generative AI agents was the original motivation, but most of the work since has been on the OS itself, and the AI parts are ordinary file servers. For example, llmsrv at /mnt/llm and speech9p are started from the login profile, and if you delete those lines they're simply not there. There's also non-generative AI additions on object detection served as files at /mnt/vision, on the CPU or a GPU host, and voice calls between devices done by mounting each other's audio files over 9P. There's a GUI layer intended to facilitate hands-free AI agent use, but it too is optional." He also said that InferNode's development was largely independent of the existing efforts, partly because the primary target was Arm64, not x86-64. Its 64-bit Dis runtime is incompatible with the 32-bit original: "The opcodes, file format and magic number are unchanged, but the word size isn't, so frame sizes, offsets and pointer maps all differ. Limbo source recompiles without edits. A 32-bit .dis is currently rejected at load time." InferNode doesn't implement 9front's DP9IK authentication protocol , so it cannot connect to servers requiring that authentication. Dr Finn told us: "DP9IK is not quantum-safe. That's the reason. InferNode's current crypto policy is strict CNSA ." InferNode also includes some slightly unexpected components, related to its intended use for testing LLM agents – such as a wallet for the Ethereum cryptocurrency, which Finn said was "mainly to support agent payments." The first release of Inferno was in 1996, the year after Java and the JVM were launched. Inferno is a much more ambitious project, but its core function – the ability to run identical binaries on multiple platforms, without recompilation – was close enough that they ended up competing in the market, and Java won. It was a pleasant surprise to see a modernized version of Inferno arrive this year, 30 years on. Finn told us: "About a year ago I saw the potential for a 'break-out' moment for this tech as a runtime for containing AI agents. The flood of cybersecurity risks we would face on account of adversarial AI agents required new systems with small footprints and minimal attack surfaces. Inferno was a perfect candidate and it was an opportunity to show the world how visionary Plan 9's ideas were and how well they mapped on to pressing contemporary security issues." "If InferNode succeeds, it is an opportunity for Plan 9's ideas to migrate out of hobby-land and really make an impact – as they deservedly should." He has a point. On a related note, this vulture discussed the possibility of rebuilding the world's IT systems from scratch on last week's Kettle podcast . Perhaps the hour for tools like this really has come round at last. ®

title: Microsoft refreshes Copilot app search for users without an AI subscription
summary: Meanwhile, Google's homepage demo leaves a familiar button out of the picture
content: Microsoft is updating search in its Microsoft 365 Copilot app for users without a Copilot license, with a toggle to restore the classic interface. Google, meanwhile, is giving AI searches more prominence on its homepage, where the familiar Search button is absent from a newly demonstrated layout. Microsoft's change is rolling out now and will hit Deferred Release by mid-January 2027. It will impact users with a Microsoft 365 license who do not have a Copilot license and "provides modern search controls to help users find, refine, and navigate search results more easily." It's enabled by default, which is a shame since administrators would likely prefer an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, and users can switch back to the "classic search experience" via a toggle on the search results page. Microsoft has not specified how long this toggle will remain available. Its separate Copilot Search experience had a fallback toggle scheduled for removal 60 days after general availability. "With the updated search experience, users can continue to find files using keywords, use modern search controls to refine and navigate results, and search supported connected third-party content when their organization has configured connected sources," Microsoft said. The results will still only display content to which users have permission. Microsoft advises administrators to brief users and help desks on the changed interface and the option to switch back. Microsoft's search tweaks arrive as the future of the Google Search button on Google's desktop homepage looks uncertain. In a post , Google VP of Product Robby Stein described a collapsible sidebar that lists users' recent AI conversations, pushing AI deeper into the search experience. Stein called it "a much simpler way to pick up where you left off," and said it would help customers "easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches." However, something else was obvious in Stein's post: the Google Search button was not present. Stein explained in August that Google had performed a "small test on desktop to help people find new things they can do with Search." Part of that test was the removal of the Google Search button. Users can still submit queries by pressing Enter. Stein said the test would have "no impact to how the core search works." The sidebar rollout doesn't itself confirm the Search button's permanent retirement. For now, its absence from Stein's demonstration is another sign of which features Google wants users to notice. ®

title: BepiColombo takes the long way around Mercury after software glitch
summary: Shortened burn leaves probe in a 75-hour orbit, but ESA says December separation remains on schedule
content: A software fault cut short BepiColombo's Mercury orbit insertion burn, but the European Space Agency (ESA) says the mission remains on track to separate its two science orbiters on December 9. ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), still carrying JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), fired its four axial thrusters on November 21 to place the spacecraft in orbit. The burn began at 1824 UTC, when BepiColombo was approximately 635 km above the planet's surface. It was supposed to last for 37 minutes but shut down early . The shutdown , caused by a software issue involving attitude guidance and thruster control, left the spacecraft in safe mode, a protective state in which all non-essential activities cease. Ignacio Tanco, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Operations Director, said: "Upon finding Bepi in safe mode, it was like flipping a switch. Everybody was focused in understanding what had happened." The burn achieved around 77 percent of the planned velocity change, securing an orbit around Mercury but leaving BepiColombo taking 75 hours to circle the planet instead of the intended 58. The good news is that multiple burns were always going to be needed to adjust the orbit ahead of Mio separation and MPO reaching its science orbit. "The remaining MOI [Mercury Orbit Insertion] sequence has already been adapted to the new trajectory, with no additional burns required," ESA said. "After each burn, the Flight Dynamics team determines the achieved orbit to then design the next manoeuvre," said Frank Budnik, ESA's BepiColombo Flight Dynamics Manager. "So, the sequence is not only more propellant-efficient, it also allows Flight Dynamics to adapt each subsequent burn to the spacecraft's actual trajectory. It's a dynamic sequence! Each new manoeuvre is based on the previous ones." Teams at ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) and Airbus continue to investigate the underlying software fault. ESA has not said whether the revised burn sequence will affect propellant reserves available for a possible mission extension. The separation of Mio and MPO is planned for December 9, and more burns will be needed to guide MPO to its final orbit by March 2027, with science operations starting in April 2027. ®

title: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
summary: No sophisticated malware or attack framework required
content: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes. It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine. “What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register . “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.” Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register , Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one. Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET. 'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking' OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work. “Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.” That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing. The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t). After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works. The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems. “It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.” 'No blocklist would have helped' In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit. It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then. The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.” While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein. “No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.” Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds. “Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
summary: ‘Shirudo’ project promises to whip up compensating controls in a hurry
content: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium , a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed. “Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production. Shirudo is open source and available here . The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation. Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls. Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source , and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it. That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®

title: CrowdStrike splashes $44B on Zscaler, customers brace for the bill
summary: Record-breaking cybersecurity deal promises tighter integration, but sysadmins fear higher prices and vendor lock-in
content: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals. The all-stock deal, announced on Monday , will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz . Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The plan is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them. Naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system." The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers. Some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before. "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration issues, etc," wrote one sysadmin. Another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun." CrowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product. Others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete. There may also be some nervous employees at both companies. CrowdStrike is targeting $500 million in annual cost savings within two years of completing the acquisition, identifying datacenter infrastructure, supplier spending, and wider operations as areas where it can trim the fat. Neither company disclosed whether that would involve job cuts. Then there's the matter of putting more of the world's corporate security infrastructure in the hands of CrowdStrike, whose botched July 2024 software update took down an estimated 8.5 million Windows machines , grounding flights and disrupting hospitals, banks, and businesses worldwide. The incident gave IT departments a rather painful lesson in the risks of relying heavily on a single technology supplier. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, assuming regulators and Zscaler shareholders give it the green light. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry will remain in charge of the business and take a seat on CrowdStrike's board. CrowdStrike reckons the combined business will have more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue when the deal closes. Judging by the reaction from some customers, they'll be keeping a particularly close eye on how much of that revenue comes from them. ®

title: Orgs that leak data 'prioritize corporate interests over customers' says Have I Been Pwned’s Troy Hunt
summary: Leakers move through denial, bargaining, delay, legal threats, then claiming Hunt is the real villain
content: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all. Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.” Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.” Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms. Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.” Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.” Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed. If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter. Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.” Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach. Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless. Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways: Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it; Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site; Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm. Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.” The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers. A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text. The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well. “Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.” Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.” Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “ absolutely nails it! ” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

title: 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters
content: Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise. In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name . Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests. Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.” The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote. Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.” “Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.” To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters. That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients , university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs. And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation. Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility. Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

title: 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front
summary: A spatial classic Finder in the style of A/UX
content: Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful. 9/UX is a new project by Jeff " Progrium " Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more. When you follow that link, and you should, pay close attention to what looks like a screenshot at the top. It is not an image. It's a real live executing instance of the OS, running inside your web browser, running on top of hyper9 . (That is worth reading too – it's an impressive project in its own right.) As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front." The README provides more detail: "9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop experience (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata." Lindsay introduced 9/UX earlier this month in a short X thread , saying he "made my own kind of A/UX but on Plan 9." In its creator's own words, "it's slop", but this is kind of interesting, original, creative bot-assisted coding that we enjoy looking at. At the end of last week, he returned to explain more : "9/UX isn’t just a pretty Mac-style UI on Plan 9. It's filesystem inspectable. Shell scriptable. Even the Mac resource file format can be used through the filesystem." Regular readers may have noticed that The Reg FOSS desk is fascinated by Plan 9 and its FOSS continuation 9front. We've written and presented at length about this remarkable OS, and tried to explain its FOSS continuation 9front several times . But even with the best will we can muster, its unique GUI is not an especially friendly or easy one. Its idiosyncratic UI was inspired by the late great Niklaus Wirth 's unbelievably tiny Oberon OS, which we have written about before . It's cryptic, and that's being generous. The research and development effort that led to Unix didn't stop when Unix 7th Edition escaped from the Bell Labs in 1981 and mutated into Unix System III. The industry enthusiastically adopted System III and later System V. A decade after 7th Edition Unix, Linux became a GPL version of something very like that traditional Unix, closely followed by the BSDs – and between them, they have very effectively distracted most of the FOSS world ever since. Even so, Research Unix lived on, saw 8th, 9th, and 10th editions, and then was replaced by Plan 9. In 1996, many of Plan 9's limitations were overcome by Inferno – whose revival as InferNode we covered this week. We always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI … But apparently not. A new, easier, and yet still simple, clean and attractive desktop for 9front is here, and it looks like classic MacOS from the era of Apple's 68030 Unix A/UX. We do not think the chances are high that the 9front community will adopt this with enthusiasm. Even so, there is an AI programming manual for agents , and we've seen some interesting looking LLM-assisted 9front apps of late. Several can be found in the agent9 distributio n , which includes LLM-assisted ports of C++ , Python , and Rust , plus a version of DOSbox , and even a package manager called pac9 .®

title: Arm strongarms site that hosts ad-free documentation and it may disappear
summary: Easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads? Down with you!
content: Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability. The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference , a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own. According to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with new CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version. “The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans. That doesn’t matter to Arm, though: As far as the lawyers are concerned, Palmisciano’s site is a copyright violation due to its use of Arm trademarks and inclusion of copyrighted reference material for the Armv9-A and Armv9-A architecture. Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else. As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form. “Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That said, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page. “I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He said that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen. Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation. "We have a responsibility to ensure Arm is the primary source of technical resources and information and to protect the Arm brand," an Arm spokesperson told us. "Striking the right balance between third parties sharing helpful peer-to-peer resources while ensuring copyrighted Arm-related technical content is accurate has been critical to building the thriving ecosystem we have today." In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month. That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us. "We have recently flagged our concerns with regard to the use of Arm copyright content and the Arm brand on this website and shared the Arm trademark guidelines," Arm explained. "Our hope is to open a constructive dialogue, and we've asked that the website owner reach out as we seek to resolve this." As Palmisciano posted on HN, Arm is asking for removal of its trademark and copyrighted documentation. That, Palmisciano said, "seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful." He also followed up around 8.30 pm GMT on Tuesday to let us know that he has not yet heard directly from Arm. ®

title: US blacklists Megaspeed hours after Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
summary: Chip boss gets his old job back, but Washington isn't done investigating one of his former flame's businesses
content: Jensen Huang was barely back in charge of Nvidia when Uncle Sam slapped Megaspeed –­ the Singaporean cloud provider at the center of the scandal that cost him his job ­­– on its trade blacklist. The US Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has added Megaspeed and a number of affiliated businesses to its Entity List, restricting their access to American technology amid an ongoing investigation into the suspected diversion of advanced GPUs to China. The final rule [PDF], filed Monday afternoon and scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on Wednesday, names seven businesses across Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand, including Megaspeed's owner, Swiftdata, and Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix. Also in Washington's crosshairs is Apex Enterprise Solutions, a Singapore-based subsidiary of Chinese cloud computing giant Alibaba. BIS said the businesses posed a significant risk of diverting advanced computing hardware to recipients or applications not authorized by the US government. Anyone looking to supply the seven companies with goods subject to US export controls will need a license, with applications subject to a "presumption of denial." Despite the timing of Monday's announcement, the US government's interest in Megaspeed predates the revelations about Jensen Huang's private life by some considerable margin. In a joint statement issued last week, the Departments of Justice and Commerce confirmed that the latter had opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 after spotting suspicious activity while monitoring potential violations of semiconductor export controls. Investigators requested records from Nvidia relating to both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed in May 2025, and the GPU giant put the Singaporean outfit on its internal "no sell" list the following month. US investigators, accompanied by Singaporean law enforcement officials, subsequently visited Megaspeed's premises and interviewed its then-CEO, Alice Huang. The Justice Department has since taken the lead on the criminal investigation. Alice Huang, who is not related to the Nvidia boss, is a businesswoman with whom Jensen was said to be having an affair – he admitted to extramarital infidelity earlier this month , although he never name-checked the Megaspeed exec. According to reports, US intelligence officials suspected she was working on behalf of Chinese intelligence, though Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations. Megaspeed maintains that its business is lawful and says Alice Huang formally left the company in August last year. It has also enlisted outside lawyers to conduct an internal investigation. Nvidia's own Huang lasted all of 11 days in corporate exile. The chipmaker's board unanimously voted to reinstate its co-founder as president and CEO on Monday, less than a week after board chairman Harvey Jones indicated that bringing him back wasn't on the cards. The U-turn followed a lobbying campaign by some of Silicon Valley's biggest names, including Elon Musk , and some rather more consequential intervention from the White House. President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia's directors to give Huang his job back. Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from senior US government officials regarding the national security implications of Huang's return. There are still plenty of people in Washington who have questions for Huang, however. The Nvidia boss is due to sit down with three congressional committees on December 1, with the chipmaker's general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to face lawmakers the following day. Nvidia has also established a board-level committee to oversee national security and export control compliance, putting its trade compliance personnel under the supervision of three directors. Nvidia shareholders may be delighted to have Jensen back, but the returning CEO has barely a week to prepare for his congressional grilling over the affair that helped bring about his departure. ®
